scientific_corrections: Park et al. explicitly discuss censoring effects; previous claim that they omitted this removed.

new_citation_claims.title: Explainable AI for survival analysis: a median-SHAP approach
manuscript_paragraphs: Ter-Minassian et al. \cite{ref7} show that Shapley interpretations also depend on the summary of the prediction distribution and the reference against which contributions are measured. Their median-SHAP approach is designed for models predicting individual survival times. Langbein et al. \cite{ref61} review interpretable machine learning for survival analysis and illustrate several methods with GBSG2. Together, these papers show why two attribution methods can produce different summaries without either being incorrectly calculated: they may explain different outputs, use different references, or aggregate across time and patients differently.

new_citation_claims.title: Data mining and machine learning in cancer survival research: An overview and future recommendations,
manuscript_paragraphs: Huang et al. \cite{ref1} review survival prediction using real-world healthcare data. They describe substantial variation in clinical conditions, sample sizes, algorithms, validation and performance measures, with random survival forests and neural networks appearing frequently. Kaur, Doja and Ahmad \cite{ref8} similarly review data-mining and machine-learning approaches in cancer survival research. Together, these reviews establish the breadth of the field, but the diversity of their included studies makes a single pooled ordering of algorithms inappropriate. A reported improvement depends on the endpoint, predictors and comparison against which it was obtained.

new_citation_claims.title: Machine learning and deep learning to improve overall survival prediction in cervical cancer patients,
manuscript_paragraphs: Clinical applications add detail that broad rankings cannot capture. Jiang et al. \cite{ref9} compare machine-learning and DeepSurv models for cervical-cancer survival using clinical and tumour characteristics. Kim et al. \cite{ref77} compare deep learning, Cox regression and RSF in oral cancer. Matysiak, Hojdis and Szewczuk \cite{ref12} use Cox regression and RSF to study immune-nutritional predictors in advanced gastric cancer. These studies share a prognostic aim, but differ in patient selection, clinical variables, follow-up and model development. Their findings motivate testing flexible methods in several clinical settings while keeping the comparison within each cohort consistent.

new_citation_claims.title: Artificial neural networks for diagnosis and survival prediction in colon cancer,
manuscript_paragraphs: Kantidakis, Hazewinkel and Fiocco \cite{ref5} critically review neural networks for medical survival prediction. They describe a range of architectures and assess the assumptions, validation and reporting of the applied studies. Their review helps explain why neural-model results cannot be interpreted independently of the event definition, training sample and development procedure. Ahmed's earlier review of neural networks in colon-cancer diagnosis and survival \cite{ref10} shows that interest in nonlinear prognostic relationships predates DeepSurv. The newer architectures expand the available representations, while the need to specify the prediction target and evaluate on held-out data remains.

new_citation_claims.title: Reporting of prognostic clinical prediction models based on machine learning methods in oncology needs to be improved,
manuscript_paragraphs: Clear reporting is part of making such evidence interpretable. Dhiman et al. \cite{ref35} document incomplete reporting in oncology prediction models developed using machine learning. Their review supports explicit descriptions of predictor handling, model development, validation and performance assessment. These details allow readers to distinguish an improvement due to a learning method from one arising from a different feature set or evaluation procedure. The methodological contribution of a controlled comparison therefore includes making those choices common and visible, alongside reporting the predictive results.

new_citation_claims.title: Comparison of time-to-event machine learning models in predicting oral cavity cancer prognosis,
manuscript_paragraphs: Applied comparisons illustrate the consequences of using several domains. Adeoye et al. \cite{ref36} also evaluated several neural and forest models for oral-cavity cancer using concordance and Brier error. Such studies show why the model with the strongest discrimination need not produce the best-calibrated probabilities. new_citation_claims.title: Survival prediction models: an introduction to discrete-time modeling,
manuscript_paragraphs: Kvamme and Borgan \cite{ref21} compare continuous- and discrete-time neural survival models. They show why the likelihood and time representation are substantive modelling decisions. Suresh, Severn and Ghosh \cite{ref46} explain how discrete-time hazards can be fitted through a person-period representation, permitting binary-learning methods to model interval event probabilities. Interval boundaries affect the representation of event timing and the reconstructed survival curve. A piecewise-exponential model also uses intervals, but specifies a continuous-time event process with constant hazard within each interval; it is not simply a binary classifier applied to the original patient records.

new_citation_claims.title: Survival Analysis as Imprecise Classification with Trainable Kernels,
manuscript_paragraphs: Other formulations handle censored event times through imprecise probabilities. In the present comparison, DeepSurv supplies a nonlinear proportional-hazards predictor, while the Bayesian models use an explicit piecewise baseline. Training-derived time intervals and shared evaluation times make the role of that representation clear.

new_citation_claims.title: BHCox: Bayesian heredity-constrained Cox proportional hazards models for detecting gene-environment interactions,
manuscript_paragraphs: Sun et al.'s BHCox study \cite{ref52} is especially close to the present prior comparison. It develops heredity-constrained Bayesian proportional-hazards models with spike-and-slab and regularised horseshoe priors for gene--environment interactions. Its baseline hazard uses M-splines, while heredity constraints link interaction effects to their main effects. The related BHAFT study \cite{ref68} examines heredity-constrained shrinkage in an accelerated failure-time formulation. These studies establish that comparing structured shrinkage priors in survival models is already an active research direction. They also identify the distinction relevant here: a low-dimensional clinical main-effects comparison, with a common piecewise-exponential baseline and a Normal reference, asks a different question from selecting high-dimensional interactions.
new_citation_claims.source_anchor: Methods: Heredity-constrained Cox proportional hazard model; Prior distribution; MCMC sampling; Simulation study; Real data analysis; Discussion
new_citation_claims.original_claim_fit_assessment: Essential close related work, not a disposable application citation. Distinguish its heredity-constrained high-dimensional interaction target and M-spline baseline from the common piecewise-exponential main-effects comparison here. Do not claim the thesis first compares these prior families.

new_citation_claims.title: Bayesian inference using Hamiltonian Monte\textendash{}Carlo algorithm for nonlinear joint modeling in the context of cancer immunotherapy,
manuscript_paragraphs: Alvares et al. \cite{ref90} review Bayesian survival analysis using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. INLA provides deterministic approximate inference for suitable latent Gaussian model structures, offering a different computational route from MCMC. Kerioui et al. \cite{ref58}, by contrast, use Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for nonlinear joint modelling of tumour dynamics and survival in cancer immunotherapy. Together, these studies show that the inference method depends on the model's structure as well as its scientific purpose. This thesis uses NUTS to sample the specified hierarchical models and evaluates computational reliability alongside prediction, since posterior summaries require adequately explored parameter distributions.

new_citation_claims.original_claim_fit_assessment: Preserve Bayesian computation/joint-model context. It is not an empirical Cox-versus-RSF benchmark or a universal performance-ranking source.

new_citation_claims.title: Comparison of nomogram with random survival forest for prediction of survival in patients with spindle cell carcinoma,
manuscript_paragraphs: Baralou, Kalpourtzi and Touloumi \cite{ref37} compare Cox regression and random forests through simulation. Such comparisons help identify when the additional flexibility is useful: nonlinear effects and interactions provide opportunities for tree-based methods, while simpler relationships may be represented efficiently by a suitable Cox model. Sample size, censoring and tuning influence the balance. In applied spindle-cell carcinoma modelling, Zhang et al. \cite{ref79} report comparable prediction from a Cox nomogram and RSF. Taken together, these studies support including both model classes and assessing their probability predictions, rather than assuming a general replacement of Cox regression by forests.

new_citation_claims.title: A novel Bayesian continuous piecewise linear log\textendash{}hazard model, with estimation and inference via reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo,
manuscript_paragraphs: Chapple, Peak and Hemal \cite{ref91} extend the piecewise-exponential approach through a continuous piecewise-linear log-hazard model fitted using reversible-jump MCMC. Their formulation allows the hazard representation itself to adapt, whereas the present study uses a fixed number of training-derived intervals. These alternatives illustrate two separate places to introduce flexibility: the baseline and the predictor effects. Keeping the baseline common here concentrates the prior comparison on regression coefficients, while retaining an explicit model for absolute survival.

new_citation_claims.title: Extending beyond Bagust and Beale: Fully parametric piecewise exponential models for extrapolation of survival outcomes in health technology assessment,
manuscript_paragraphs: Freeman et al. \cite{ref92} compare flexible parametric, piecewise-exponential and fractional-polynomial approaches for Bayesian pairwise meta-analysis under non-proportional hazards. Their simulations examine restricted mean survival and extrapolation under limited follow-up. Cooney and White \cite{ref93} investigate fully parametric piecewise-exponential extrapolation for health technology assessment. Both studies show why assumptions beyond the observed follow-up can have a substantial role when the target extends into the survival tail. The current predictive assessment instead concentrates on horizons supported by the training and validation follow-up.

new_citation_claims.original_claim_fit_assessment: This paper concerns change-point estimation and health-technology-assessment extrapolation, not horseshoe shrinkage. Appropriate baseline/tail context, with extrapolation distinguished from within-follow-up prediction.

new_citation_claims.title: Bayesian Inference for High Dimensional Cox Models with Gaussian and Diffused-Gamma Priors: A Case Study of Mortality in COVID-19 Patients Admitted to the ICU,
manuscript_paragraphs: Song, Guha and Li \cite{ref94} investigate Gaussian and diffused-gamma priors in high-dimensional Cox models using partial likelihood. Mu et al. \cite{ref95} combine horseshoe sparsity with a point-mass mixture for spatial variation in Cox coefficients. Their two-stage approach uses site-specific partial-likelihood information before MCMC estimation. These approaches broaden the prior literature beyond a single type of sparsity, but also show why likelihood and coefficient structure must be specified when comparing findings. Spatially varying effects, interaction heredity and ordinary main effects produce different posterior interpretation tasks.

new_citation_claims.title: Sparsity information and regularization in the horseshoe and other shrinkage priors
manuscript_paragraphs: The regularised horseshoe provides strong shrinkage of small effects while allowing larger effects through local scales and a finite slab \cite{piironen2017}. Its behaviour depends on the global scale, local scales and slab specification, as well as on the data. Similarly, the spike-and-slab label can refer to a point mass, a latent selection model, or a continuous mixture of narrow and wide components. In this thesis, the continuous mixture has Beta-distributed variance weights; those weights are not posterior probabilities that a coefficient is exactly zero or included in a selected model.
